Text: A {{c1::local variable}} is declared inside a method, constructor, or block.
Extra: Local variables must be assigned before use.

Text: An {{c1::instance variable}} belongs to an object.
Extra: Each object has its own instance field values.

Text: A {{c1::static variable}} belongs to the class, not an individual object.
Extra: Static state is shared at the class level.

Text: `final` means a variable can be assigned {{c1::only once}}.
Extra: After assignment, reassignment is not allowed.

Text: For reference variables, `final` prevents {{c1::reassignment}}, not necessarily object mutation.
Extra: A mutable object can still change internally.

Text: Java constants are often declared as {{c1::static final}}.
Extra: Static for class-level sharing, final for no reassignment.

Text: Constants usually use {{c1::UPPER_SNAKE_CASE}}.
Extra: Example: `MAX_RETRY_COUNT`.

Text: A {{c1::magic number}} is a literal number used directly without a name explaining its meaning.
Extra: Named constants reduce this problem.

Text: Local variables do {{c1::not}} receive usable automatic default values.
Extra: They must be assigned before use.

Text: Reference fields default to {{c1::null}}.
Extra: Numeric fields default to zero-like values, boolean fields to false.

Text: {{c1::Scope}} is the region of code where a name can be accessed.
Extra: Scope is not lifetime.

Text: {{c1::Lifetime}} is how long a variable or object exists.
Extra: Lifetime helps explain local variables, objects, and static state.

Text: A local variable exists while its {{c1::method or block}} is executing.
Extra: After the block/method ends, the local variable is gone.

Text: An instance variable exists as long as its {{c1::object}} exists.
Extra: It is part of object state.

Text: A static variable exists as long as the {{c1::class is loaded}}.
Extra: It is class-level state.

Text: `var` was introduced in Java {{c1::10}} for local variable type inference.
Extra: `var` is not dynamic typing.

Text: `var` can be used for {{c1::local variables}}, not fields.
Extra: It requires an initializer.

Text: `var` requires an {{c1::initializer}} so the compiler can infer the type.
Extra: `var x;` is invalid.

Text: Local variables are stored on the {{c1::Stack}}, whereas objects are stored on the {{c2::Heap}}.
Extra: Stack holds transient frame data; Heap holds dynamic object instances.

Text: Class variables (static fields) are stored in the {{c1::Metaspace}} (or Method Area) of JVM memory.
Extra: They are shared by all instances and survive as long as the class remains loaded.

Text: Compiler optimizations like {{c1::constant folding}} and {{c2::constant inlining}} are enabled by marking variables as `final`.
Extra: Since the compiler knows final values won't change, it pre-computes expressions and directly inserts literal values.

Text: While the JVM automatically zero-initializes fields, stack variables require compile-time {{c1::definite assignment}} analysis to ensure safety without runtime overhead.
Extra: Zero-initializing stack frames at runtime is too slow, so Java enforces initialization statically at compile-time instead.
